title: Crates and Hipparchia
hookLine: Hipparchia chose the Cynic Crates and his poverty, and argued with philosophers as an equal (Diogenes Laërtius 6.96–98)

lines: NO HOUSE, NO MONEY, ONE CLOAK.
THE PARENTS BEG HIM TO REFUSE.
cards: A young woman from a well-off family tells her parents she's going to marry a man with no house, no money, and one worn cloak. They're horrified. They beg the man himself to talk her out of it.
He agrees, and goes to see her. What he does next turns into a marriage proposal, a very strange one, and it works. The story comes from the Cynics, the rough cousins of the Stoics.

teach.b: First, the Cynics. Their name is tied to the Greek word for dog; ancient writers give more than one reason, and it fits how they lived: in public, owning almost nothing, ignoring polite custom.
Crates of Thebes was a gentle one; he was later remembered as a kind of household friend who settled quarrels. He was also Zeno's teacher, so the Stoic porch grew partly out of his cloak.

Second, the proposal, as Diogenes Laërtius tells it. Hipparchia fell in love with Crates' talk and his way of life, and told her family she would marry no one else. Her parents asked Crates to dissuade her.
He stood in front of her, put down everything he owned, and said, in effect: here is the bridegroom, and here are his possessions; decide with that in mind.
She chose him, took up the same rough cloak, and went everywhere with him. Third, the argument.

At a dinner, she took on a philosopher called Theodorus with a neat little argument that tied him in knots. With no answer, he tried to shame her instead, quoting a line from a play: is this the woman who left her loom?
Yes, she said. Do you think I made a bad choice, spending on my education the time I'd have spent at the loom? Fourth, why she's remembered.
Hipparchia spoke as an equal, at the table and in public, and the record kept her name: Diogenes gives her a short life of her own.

how: Students of ancient philosophy read the story of Crates and Hipparchia in Diogenes Laërtius's Lives, where she is given a short life of her own.

games.q: you're Crates. a young woman wants to marry you, and her parents ask you to change her mind. what do you do?
o: show her everything you own and let her decide.
games.why: Crates put down all his possessions and said, here is the bridegroom, and these are his goods. she chose him anyway.

practice: Picture a room you're in this week where you tend to go quiet, a meeting, a family dinner, a class, and notice where the shrinking happens: your shoulders, your throat.
Now picture saying one thing you actually think, plainly, without apology and without attack, not to win, just to be in the conversation as an equal. Feel your feet on the floor while you imagine it.

wordCard.voice: Hipparchia. She chose the Cynic Crates over her family's wishes, and argued with philosophers at the table as an equal. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: dog. The word the name Cynic is tied to, a name given to philosophers who lived in public and scorned custom.

carryVoice: Your line: as an equal. She chose the cloak, and she kept her voice. Day six hundred forty-nine, done.
